scenarios.title: A timeout after provider acceptance
scenarios.description: Watch internal uncertainty differ from the external fake ledger. A stable key can help only when the provider actually supports its read-only lookup contract.

steps.title: One delivery identity is ready
steps.note: The example starts after ingestion. Repeated queue work refers to this same delivery; it is not another email request identity.

steps.title: A claims and passes the current preference gate
steps.note: The provider key and request bytes are frozen. No provider call runs inside the engine's monitor.

steps.title: Provider accepts, but the response is lost
steps.note: The fake provider ledger has one accepted message. The service only knows an uncertain outcome and schedules a bounded retry for t=1000 ms.

steps.title: The retry is not due yet
steps.note: At t=999 the original retry time has not arrived. No additional provider request is made.

steps.title: The same key returns the original provider ID
steps.reason: provider accepted; not proof of delivery or read
steps.note: A read-only lookup recovers the original ID while retained; it can never create a second send. This does not prove mailbox delivery or user read.

scenarios.title: Opt-out arrives while work waits
scenarios.description: Preferences are checked before each send authorization, rather than only when an event enters the queue.

steps.title: A claims queued work
steps.note: Claiming is not permission to skip current preferences. No external attempt has been authorized.

steps.title: The customer disables the channel
steps.note: The delivery is still claimed, but the authoritative preference changed before its final authorization gate.

steps.title: The fresh gate suppresses the attempt
steps.note: There are zero provider calls. A request already authorized or in flight would have a different boundary and could not be recalled.

scenarios.title: A stale worker cannot overwrite its replacement
scenarios.description: A 30-second lease and claim epoch control local ownership. They do not undo an external call that already happened.

steps.title: A's external call accepted; completion is delayed
steps.note: The provider ledger has one acceptance, but the local row is still SENDING. Simulate a paused worker before it records the response.

steps.title: The live lease cannot be taken
steps.note: At t=29999 another worker cannot own this row. Provider latency does not turn queue redelivery into new permission.

steps.title: At lease equality B becomes the owner
steps.note: Reclaiming a SENDING row advances the claim epoch and preserves uncertainty about its external side effect.

steps.title: A's late update is fenced; its evidence is retained
steps.note: The dispatch state stays owned by B. A deduplicated acceptance observation is still retained; fencing state is not permission to erase an external fact.

steps.title: B resolves with the same immutable provider key
steps.reason: provider accepted; not proof of delivery or read
steps.note: The old epoch does not create a new provider identity. The read-only lookup returns its original ID, leaving one physical acceptance.

scenarios.title: No safe replay contract means no blind retry
scenarios.description: The chosen policy favors a visible unresolved reminder over inventing exactly-once behavior for an uncertain provider.

steps.title: This adapter has no safe replay window
steps.note: The delivery records zero lookup-history milliseconds. A stable local key alone does not make the external provider deduplicate.

steps.title: An unknown outcome becomes reconciliation work
steps.note: The fake accepted one message before the timeout. The service cannot safely guess whether another call would duplicate it, so it quarantines rather than blindly resends.

steps.title: Automatic queue redelivery does not resend
steps.note: Provider calls remain one. A real reconciler needs lookup/callback evidence or a recorded operator decision; a new key is not a safe generic repair.
